tips.0: Focus on the eye nearest the camera — at wide apertures the depth of field is only a few centimeters.
tips.1: Step back and zoom in (85mm+) for flattering compression; wide lenses up close distort facial features.

tips.0: Focus about one-third into the scene or use the hyperfocal distance for front-to-back sharpness.
tips.1: Shoot from a tripod with the self-timer or a remote to eliminate shake at slow shutter speeds.

tips.0: Zone focus: pre-set focus at 3m and f/8, and everything from 2m to 6m will be sharp — no AF delay.
tips.1: Auto ISO with a minimum shutter speed of 1/250s freezes walking subjects while you concentrate on framing.

tips.0: Match shutter speed to subject: 1/1000s for perched birds, 1/2500s or faster for birds in flight.
tips.1: Shoot at eye level and wait for head turns — a catchlight in the eye brings the image to life.

tips.0: Pre-focus where the action will happen (the goal, the apex of a corner) and start the burst just before the peak.
tips.1: Panning at 1/60s–1/125s with continuous AF blurs the background while keeping the subject sharp.

tips.1: Diffraction bites hard beyond f/16; use focus stacking instead of stopping down further.

tips.1: Focus manually on a bright star using magnified live view; set white balance near 3900K for a neutral sky.

what-settings-for-portraits.question: What camera settings should I use for portraits?
what-settings-for-portraits.answer: Start with a wide aperture (f/1.8–f/2.8) for background blur, a shutter speed of at least 1/200s to avoid motion blur, and the lowest ISO the light allows (100–400). Use single-point autofocus on the nearest eye, or eye-detection AF if your camera has it.

what-settings-for-milky-way.question: What settings do I need to photograph the Milky Way?
what-settings-for-milky-way.answer: A wide, fast lens at its widest aperture (f/1.4–f/2.8), a 10–25 second exposure (longer trails the stars), ISO 1600–6400, manual focus set on a bright star, and a tripod. A moonless night far from city lights matters more than any camera setting.

are-cheat-sheet-settings-exact.question: Are these settings exact recipes?
are-cheat-sheet-settings-exact.answer: No — they are proven starting points. Light varies enormously between scenes, so treat the ranges as a first guess, take a test shot, check the histogram, and adjust. The goal is to get you into the right neighborhood fast, not to replace judgment.
